Conclusion: the spread of NAD(P)-binding enzymes across several distinct SCOPe folds and superfamilies shows that the ability to bind this cofactor arose more than once (convergent evolution), while the shared ancestry that SCOP actually asserts is confined to within each superfamily (divergent evolution). Cofactor binding or active-site similarity alone cannot establish homology because it is a functional, selectable property that different scaffolds can reach independently.

What SCOPe 2.08 shows. In class c (alpha and beta proteins, a/b), NAD(P)-dependent enzymes are classified in several folds that SCOP treats as unrelated: fold c.2 'NAD(P)-binding Rossmann-fold domains' (sunid 51734, with its single superfamily c.2.1, sunid 51735, containing families such as c.2.1.1 alcohol dehydrogenase-like C-terminal domain, c.2.1.2 tyrosine-dependent oxidoreductases, c.2.1.3 GAPDH-like N-terminal domain, c.2.1.4 formate/glycerate dehydrogenases NAD-domain, c.2.1.5 LDH N-terminal domain-like, c.2.1.6 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase-like, c.2.1.7 amino acid dehydrogenase-like, c.2.1.8 CoA-binding domain, c.2.1.9 potassium channel NAD-binding domain, c.2.1.11 siroheme synthase N-terminal domain-like, c.2.1.12 Rex C-terminal domain, c.2.1.13 ornithine cyclodeaminase-like, c.2.1.0 automated matches); fold c.3 'FAD/NAD(P)-binding domain' (sunid 51904, superfamily c.3.1, sunid 51905); fold c.4 'Nucleotide-binding domain' (sunid 51970, superfamily c.4.1, sunid 51971, with families such as adrenodoxin reductase N-terminal domain, D-amino acid oxidase N-terminal domain, UDP-galactopyranose mutase N-terminal domain); fold c.1 'TIM beta/alpha-barrel' (sunid 51350), which contains superfamily c.1.7 'NAD(P)-linked oxidoreductase' (sunid 51430, aldo-keto reductases); fold c.71 'Dihydrofolate reductase-like' (sunid 53596), whose enzymes use NADPH; fold c.82 'ALDH-like' (sunid 53719), the NAD(P)-dependent aldehyde dehydrogenases; and fold c.23 'Flavodoxin-like' (sunid 52171) with superfamily c.23.5 'Flavoproteins' (sunid 52218). In class d, fold d.81 'FwdE/GAPDH domain-like' (sunid 55346) holds the catalytic domain that partners with the c.2.1.3 Rossmann NAD-binding domain in GAPDH. These folds have different beta-sheet topologies and strand orders, and SCOP does not place them under a common superfamily. Note that c.2, c.3 and c.4 share the classic dinucleotide-binding motif (beta-alpha-beta unit with a glycine-rich loop contacting the pyrophosphate), yet SCOP keeps them as separate folds because the overall sheet topology differs and the similarity is confined to a short substructure that could reflect either very ancient divergence or independent recruitment of a favorable supersecondary motif; SCOP deliberately does not assert homology across them.

Evolutionary strength by level. Family (e.g. c.2.1.1) implies clear sequence-detectable common ancestry. Superfamily (e.g. c.2.1, c.3.1, c.4.1, c.1.7) is SCOP's homology assertion: low sequence identity but structural and functional features that indicate a probable common origin, which is divergent evolution. Fold (c.2 vs c.3 vs c.4 vs c.1 vs c.71 vs c.82 vs c.23) implies only the same major secondary-structure arrangement and topology; it carries no claim of common ancestry and may reflect physics-driven convergence onto favorable architectures. Class (c) implies only secondary-structure composition. The fact that NAD(P) binding is distributed over at least seven class c folds plus others therefore means that, at the level SCOP recognizes homology, NAD(P)-dependent oxidoreductases are a polyphyletic set: within c.2.1 all the dehydrogenase NAD-domains are homologous and diverged, but c.2.1 versus c.1.7 versus c.82.1 versus c.71.1 represent independent inventions of NAD(P) binding (convergence). Even within the TIM barrel fold c.1, the NAD(P)-linked oxidoreductase superfamily c.1.7 is one of many superfamilies, so the fold is shared by enzymes with unrelated cofactor chemistry while the cofactor is shared with enzymes of unrelated folds. Both directions of mismatch show that cofactor and fold are independent variables.

Why cofactor or active-site similarity alone is insufficient for homology. (1) Strong functional constraint drives convergence: NAD(P) is an ancient, abundant metabolite with a fixed chemistry (adenine, two phosphates, ribose, nicotinamide), so any scaffold that evolves to use it will converge on similar features, such as a glycine-rich loop or helix dipole stabilizing the pyrophosphate, an acidic residue on the adenine ribose 2'-OH for NAD specificity or a basic patch for the 2'-phosphate of NADP, and a hydrophobic cleft for the nicotinamide. These are predictable chemical solutions, not inherited characters. (2) Active sites are small, and small motifs recur by chance or selection: catalytic triads, the Ser/Tyr/Lys of short-chain dehydrogenases versus the Tyr/Lys/His/Asp of aldo-keto reductases, and the dinucleotide-binding motif all occupy a handful of residues on different folds. The same catalytic residues on different topologies are a textbook signature of convergence. (3) Homology requires evidence of common descent in the whole domain: shared fold topology, conserved core packing, statistically significant sequence similarity or profile/HMM links, conserved unusual structural features that are not required by function, and consistent domain architecture or gene context. SCOP groups into a superfamily only when such function-independent similarity is present; it explicitly refuses to merge folds on the basis of function alone. (4) Homology is also not transitive through function: a protein that binds NAD and a Rossmann-fold protein are not thereby homologous, and a shared Rossmann fold is itself not proof of homology because the fold is a common, 'superfold' architecture that may have arisen more than once. (5) Transferring function the other way is equally unsafe: members of c.2.1 include the potassium channel NAD-binding domain, Rex repressor and the CoA-binding domain, so even within a true homologous superfamily the cofactor and catalytic function are not conserved. Therefore, to claim homology between two NAD(P)-binding enzymes one needs, beyond the cofactor, independent evidence such as significant sequence or profile similarity, equivalent beta-sheet topology and core, and shared non-functional structural idiosyncrasies; to claim a shared function one needs conserved catalytic residues and experimental evidence, not just superfamily membership.

Limits. SCOPe 2.08 node descriptions and hierarchy were used as the public record; the statements about which families lie under c.2.1 and c.4.1 come directly from the release 2.08 children listings. The c.2.1 and c.3.1 annotation sections contain no curator comments in this release, so the convergence-versus-divergence interpretation rests on the hierarchy itself (separate folds, no shared superfamily) and on general structural-biology knowledge, and classification of some automated-match members (c.2.1.0) is less reliable than curated families.

Conclusion: the spread of NAD(P)-binding enzymes across several distinct SCOPe folds and superfamilies shows that the ability to bind this cofactor arose more than once (convergent evolution), while the shared ancestry that SCOP actually asserts is confined to within each superfamily (divergent evolution).
